extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary criticism, critics, playwrights, and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical principles for assessing dramatic works (tragedy, stage-plays) with attention to dramatic probability, character construction, moral purpose, stagecraft, and poetic diction. Drawn from close critical commentary on specific plays and general theory of dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic probability
rubrics_metrics.description: “On this propensity, so deeply rooted in our nature, a specific dramatic probability may be raised by a true poet, if the whole of his work be in harmony: a dramatic probability, sufficient for dramatic pleasure, even when the component characters and incidents border on impossibility.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet need not force literal belief; he must obtain a state in the audience where they 'yield themselves to a dream' and suspend judgment. Dramatic probability is achieved when the whole work coheres so that even improbable incidents feel fitting and pleasurable (example: Don John and his statue-ghost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding supernatural effects (motivation and cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is a mere supernatural effect, without even a hint of any supernatural agency; a prodigy, without any circumstance mentioned that is prodigious; and a miracle introduced without a ground, and ending without a result.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supernatural or prodigious events require hinted agency, antecedent preparation, or causal context; miracles introduced gratuitously (scene-for-scene spectacle) disrupt dramatic probability and leave the audience unsatisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony and unity of the whole work
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic effects (probability, supernatural, character actions) depend upon the whole work being 'in harmony.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All parts — incidents, character, diction, stage-effects — must cohere; isolated displays of prowess or novelty undermine the work unless they serve the unified design and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency and intelligible motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of characters whose actions are not in keeping with their established roles (example: the Prior who only scolds yet never acts, then suddenly weeps and kneels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters must behave in ways intelligible to the audience given their past conduct, social roles, and motives. Sudden revolutions of temperament or implausible inaction break credibility and lessen dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral purpose and representation of vice
rubrics_metrics.description: The play's moral function: to display the hollowness of showy instrumental qualities (honour, courage) when presented as substitutes for virtue, rather than to reward or glamorize criminals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a drama depicts courage, honour, or gentlemanly qualities in villains, it should ultimately expose their emptiness when detached from virtue—drama should not confuse cause and effect or reward criminality with sympathetic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and balance of traits in character construction
rubrics_metrics.description: “The ingredients too are mixed in the happiest proportion, so as to uphold and relieve each other--more especially in that constant interpoise of wit, gaiety, and social generosity, which prevents the criminal ... from sinking into the mere ruffian.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give even immoral characters qualities (wit, gaiety, generosity) in balanced measure so they remain interesting and plausible without becoming attractive endorsements of vice; composition of traits should preserve imaginative judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'scene for the sake of a scene' (spectacle without purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The storm-scene and other striking tableaux are criticized as 'a scene for the sake of a scene' — a rarity without precedent which, though admired, may be 'innocent' of dramatic foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacular or novel scenes must serve the story or thematic design; purely spectacular passages that do not advance cause/effect or deepen character feel gratuitous and can be disruptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausible stagecraft and socially plausible actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples where stage actions are implausible given social roles: the Prior who knows criminals are present but does nothing (no arrests); the husband sent away at a convenient time to enable adultery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage events should respect social plausibilities and institutional responses (e.g., a Prior would act to secure the house). Logistics and social expectations must be considered to preserve verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skillful handling of retrospective narration/exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for the Imogine scene that 'tells well and passionately the preliminary circumstances' and thus overcomes the difficulty of most first acts in giving background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background and prior events should be conveyed naturally and vividly so the audience acquires necessary information without clumsy dumps or weakening dramatic immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness and appropriateness of diction and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: The text notes 'solecisms, corrupt diction, and offences against metre' even in otherwise effective scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faults of language and metre can be outweighed by strong dramatic content, but careful attention to diction and metrical propriety strengthens dramatic authority and reader/listener reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous profanity, blasphemy, and pandering to low taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic objects to 'profane representation' (a hymn sung on stage) and to spectacle that panders to 'the grossest and most outrageous stimulants' and applauding an actor 'just been committing adultery!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of shock for its own sake or of scenes that cater to base appetite; such choices may achieve applause but can degrade moral and aesthetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide closure and intelligible outcomes for plot elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The fate of Imogine's child is left unresolved and is described as 'a riddle at the representation,' remaining unexplained after attentive perusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant plot elements introduced in a drama should have explicable outcomes or be deliberately framed as mystery; careless omission of resolution feels like an authorial lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful use of sacred or symbolic stage items
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection to the stage representation of the high altar and the singing of a hymn by chorister boys as profane stage business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sacred symbols or rituals used onstage should be handled with conscious purpose and dramatic appropriateness; careless or profane appropriation undermines seriousness and can offend audience sensibilities.
